stem: A closed economy has C=c₀+c₁Y_D, T=t₀+t₁Y, Y_D=Y−T, with c₀,t₀,t₁>0 and 0<c₁<1. Government spending Ḡ and investment Ī are exogenous. (i) Interpret t₁ and discuss whether it exceeds 1. (ii) Find equilibrium output. (iii) Find the autonomous-spending multiplier and compare t₁=0 with t₁>0.
answer: t₁ is the marginal income-tax rate, normally between 0 and 1. Y*=(c₀−c₁t₀+Ḡ+Ī)/[1−c₁(1−t₁)]. Multiplier=1/[1−c₁(1−t₁)], smaller with positive t₁.
solution: An extra rupee of income raises taxes by t₁ rupees, so t₁=dT/dY. The standard tax interpretation imposes t₁<1 so disposable income rises with income; the printed algebra alone, which states only t₁>0, does not logically forbid rates at or above 100%. Substitute disposable income (1−t₁)Y−t₀ into consumption and impose Y=C+Ḡ+Ī to obtain the formula. For positive t₁ the multiplier denominator exceeds 1−c₁, reducing responses to c₀,Ḡ or Ī. Induced tax receipts are an automatic stabilizer that leaks part of each extra income round.
hint: Substitute the tax equation into disposable income.
notes: The usual upper bound t₁<1 is an economic restriction, not a consequence of the printed inequalities.

stem: An agent maximizes log c₀+δ log c₁, 0<δ<1, subject to c₀+c₁/(1+r)=ω. (i) Find both consumption demands. (ii) How do they respond to r? (iii) When are the two consumption quantities equal?
answer: c₀=ω/(1+δ), c₁=δ(1+r)ω/(1+δ). c₀ is unchanged by r and c₁ rises with r. Equality holds iff δ(1+r)=1.
solution: Assume ω>0 and r>−1. The Euler condition is δc₀/c₁=1/(1+r), hence c₁=δ(1+r)c₀. Substituting into the budget gives the demands. Initial consumption and saving δω/(1+δ) are fixed shares of wealth; a higher return therefore leaves initial consumption unchanged and raises old-age consumption. Equality c₀=c₁ requires r=1/δ−1, independently of positive wealth. The question asks for a relationship involving wealth, but wealth cancels.
hint: Use the Euler condition and the present-value budget.

stem: A firm has F(x₁,x₂)=min(2x₁,x₁+x₂), with nonnegative inputs. (i) Describe the output-10 isoquant. (ii) Show constant returns. (iii) At input prices w₁=w₂=1, find the cost function.
answer: Isoquant: x₁=5,x₂≥5 together with x₁+x₂=10, 5≤x₁≤10. CRS holds; C(q)=q for q≥0.
solution: To produce at least 10 requires x₁≥5 and x₁+x₂≥10; equality in at least one condition gives the listed isoquant, a vertical ray from (5,5) and a descending segment to (10,0). For λ≥0, F(λx₁,λx₂)=λmin(2x₁,x₁+x₂)=λF(x₁,x₂), proving CRS. Cost at unit prices is x₁+x₂≥q. This bound is attained by every bundle x₁+x₂=q with q/2≤x₁≤q, so minimum cost is q.
hint: Translate the minimum into two output requirements.

stem: Two individuals have utilities Uᵢ=Xᵢ+Yᵢ. Initial endowments are (3,7) and (7,3). (i) Find all Pareto-optimal allocations. (ii) Find all competitive Walrasian outcomes. (iii) Are competitive outcomes Pareto optimal, and does this generalize?
answer: Every feasible allocation exhausting the aggregate (10,10) is Pareto optimal. Competitive price ratio is p_X/p_Y=1, and competitive allocations are ((x,10−x),(10−x,x)), 0≤x≤10.
solution: When all goods are allocated, U₁+U₂=20. Making one person strictly better without hurting the other would increase that sum above 20, which is impossible. Any unallocated good could instead be given to someone, so wasteful allocations are inefficient. With unequal positive prices both consumers demand only the cheaper good, preventing market clearing. At equal prices, each endowment has value 10p and each consumer can choose any bundle with Xᵢ+Yᵢ=10. Clearing both markets gives the stated line of competitive outcomes, a subset of the full efficient box. They are Pareto optimal by the sum argument and by the First Welfare Theorem: under standard competitive exchange assumptions and local nonsatiation, every competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient. Externalities, missing markets or other failures of those assumptions can invalidate the conclusion.
hint: Compare total utility, then impose individual budget balances at equal prices.

stem: A monopolist has q₁=max(10−p₁,0), q₂=max(a−p₂,0), 10<a≤20, and C(q)=5q. (i) Find optimal common price and discuss the bound a≤20. (ii) Find discriminatory prices. (iii) When is discrimination profitable? (iv) Compare consumer surplus and identify winners and losers.
answer: Let a*=10+5√2. Common price is (a+20)/4 for a<a*, or (a+5)/2 serving only market 2 for a>a*; both prices optimize at a=a*. Discriminatory prices are 7.5 and (a+5)/2. Discrimination raises profit for all a>10. Consumer effects depend on which common-price regime applies.
solution: For a common p≤10, Q=a+10−2p and profit=(p−5)Q. Its best candidate is p_B=(a+20)/4, yielding profit a²/8. The restriction a≤20 ensures this candidate is within its both-markets range; it does not ensure global optimality. For p≥10, only market 2 buys and the candidate p_H=(a+5)/2 is valid when a≥15, with profit (a−5)²/4. Comparing the two profits gives the switch a*=10+5√2≈17.071. Below it use p_B, above it use p_H; at equality either is optimal. Discrimination independently gives q₁=2.5,p₁=7.5 and q₂=(a−5)/2,p₂=(a+5)/2, with profit [25+(a−5)²]/4. Its gain over common pricing is (a−10)²/8 in the both-markets regime and 25/4 in the market-2-only regime, strictly positive for a>10. Discriminatory surpluses are CS₁=25/8 and CS₂=(a−5)²/8. Under p_B they are (20−a)²/32 and (3a−20)²/32, respectively. Market 1 benefits from discrimination and market 2 loses; total CS falls by 3(a−10)²/16. Under p_H, common-pricing surpluses are 0 and (a−5)²/8: discrimination newly serves market 1, benefits it, leaves market 2 unchanged and raises total CS by 25/8. At the switch either common-price optimum can be the comparator.
hint: Check the monopoly’s option of abandoning the smaller market, even when an interior two-market price exists.
notes: The usual interior-only answer is not globally valid for the full stated range. The source’s apparent rationale for a≤20 needs this qualification; exact piecewise solution supplied.

stem: Three zero-marginal-cost firms face p=120−q. (i) Give firm 1’s Cournot best response. (ii) Find the three-firm equilibrium. (iii) Firms 2 and 3 merge without changing marginal cost: find the new equilibrium and profit effects. Would a cartel of all firms be preferable to them?
answer: Best response q₁=max(0,(120−q₂−q₃)/2). Initially each q=30 and profit900. After merger, outsider and merged firm each q=40 and profit1600. Outsider benefits; merging firms jointly lose200. A cartel produces60 at price60 and total profit3600.
solution: Profit for firm 1 is (120−q₁−q₂−q₃)q₁, giving its best response. At a symmetric three-firm equilibrium 2q+2q=120, so each q=30, total90,p=30 and profit900. Post-merger there are two identical Cournot players; each chooses40, total80,p=40,profit1600. Firm1 gains700. Firms2 and3 previously earned1800 jointly, so their merged profit1600 is smaller: the merger is unprofitable without cost synergies. Joint monopoly/cartel revenue (120−Q)Q is maximized at Q=60,p=60,profit3600. This exceeds the initial joint2700 and post-merger joint3200, permitting a division that makes every firm better off (for example1200 each relative to the original equilibrium); cartel stability still requires preventing unilateral deviation.
hint: Treat the merged entity as one player and compare joint pre-merger profits.

stem: Production is Yₜ=0.5√Kₜ√N with fixed N; Kₜ₊₁=sYₜ+(1−δ)Kₜ. (i) Express per-worker capital change as saving minus depreciation. (ii) Find positive steady capital and output per worker. (iii) Find steady consumption per worker. (iv) Choose the saving rate maximizing it and describe a graph.
answer: Δk=0.5s√k−δk; k*=[s/(2δ)]², y*=s/(4δ), c*=s(1−s)/(4δ). Golden-rule saving rate s*=1/2.
solution: Dividing the capital equation by fixed N gives kₜ₊₁−kₜ=syₜ−δkₜ=.5s√kₜ−δkₜ. For δ>0 and s>0, a positive steady state equates these terms: √k*=s/(2δ). Then y*=.5√k*=s/(4δ), and consumption is (1−s)y*=s(1−s)/(4δ). As a function of s∈[0,1], this is a concave parabola with derivative (1−2s)/(4δ), maximized at .5. Equivalently plot production f(k)=.5√k and break-even investment δk: consumption is their vertical gap, maximized where f′(k)=δ. This gives k_GR=1/(16δ²), matched by s=.5, and maximal c=1/(16δ). Higher saving initially raises long-run productive capacity but eventually diverts too much output from consumption.
hint: Use fixed labour to divide the accumulation law, then optimize steady consumption.

stem: Ten people, five high ability and five low, live for two periods. Without college, type i earns yᵢ in each period. College in period1 gives zero earnings then, costs tuition T>0, and raises period2 earnings to (1+a)yᵢ. Lifetime payoffs are undiscounted. (i) Find schooling conditions and minimum a. (ii) Let y_H=50,y_L=40,a=3: find tuition thresholds. (iii) Tuition paid by students is subsidized to60: what happens? (iv) Government taxes earnings above50 at rate x%, wants everyone educated and must cover its tuition subsidy. Find x.
answer: School if T≤(a−1)yᵢ; necessarily a>1. Numerical thresholds: H100,L80, so both attend at tuition60. If underlying tuition cost remains T, budget balance with everyone attending requires tax fraction τ=x/100=(T−60)/130; participation requires τ≤2/11. A unique numerical x cannot be found without T or subsidy cost.
solution: Without schooling lifetime earnings are 2yᵢ; with schooling they are (1+a)yᵢ−T. Their difference is (a−1)yᵢ−T, giving the threshold. For at least one type to attend, a≥1+T/max(y_H,y_L)>1. With a=3 the thresholds are100 for H and80 for L, so higher ability is more likely to attend; at the subsidized fee60 both do. For (iv), if the real tuition cost is the original T, subsidy per student is T−60 and total cost10(T−60). With all educated, period2 earnings are200 and160; total taxable excess is5·150+5·110=1300, hence τ=(T−60)/130. High-type schooling payoff is140−150τ versus100 without school, requiring τ≤4/15. Low-type payoff is100−110τ versus80, requiring τ≤2/11, the binding condition. Thus a nonnegative self-financing subsidy with all attending exists for 60≤T≤920/11≈83.636 (strict inequalities for strict preference). T is not assigned numerically, so neither a specific percentage nor unconditional feasibility follows. If “subsidy cost” is intended differently, it must be supplied.
hint: Compare lifetime opportunity costs, then check both the government budget and individual incentives.
notes: The original tuition T or per-student government cost is not assigned, preventing a unique numerical tax. General formula and feasibility range supplied.

stem: Goods-market consumption is C=c₀+c₁(Y−T) with constant taxes and exogenous G. (i) With exogenous I, find Y and the multiplier. (ii) Replace investment with I=b₀+b₁Y−b₂i, c₁+b₁<1: find Y at given i and compare multipliers. (iii) Add M/P=d₁Y−d₂i: derive the autonomous-spending multiplier. (iv) Compare it with (i).
answer: (i) Multiplier1/(1−c₁). (ii) At fixed i,1/(1−c₁−b₁). (iii) With money equilibrium,1/[1−c₁−b₁+b₂d₁/d₂]. (iv) Relative size depends on b₁ versus b₂d₁/d₂.
solution: (i) Y=(c₀−c₁T+Ī+G)/(1−c₁). (ii) Y=(c₀−c₁T+b₀+G−b₂i)/(1−c₁−b₁). For b₁>0, the induced-investment feedback raises the fixed-interest multiplier. (iii) LM implies i=(d₁/d₂)Y−(M/P)/d₂. Substitution gives Y=[c₀−c₁T+b₀+G+(b₂/d₂)(M/P)]/[1−c₁−b₁+b₂d₁/d₂]. Differentiate with respect to c₀,b₀ or G to get the stated multiplier. (iv) Compared with1/(1−c₁), it is larger if b₁>b₂d₁/d₂, equal if they tie and smaller if b₁<b₂d₁/d₂. Induced investment amplifies spending, while higher income raises money demand and interest, crowding investment out. Positive b₂,d₁,d₂ and a positive denominator are assumed.
hint: Eliminate i using LM and compare denominators.

stem: A college must fill one seat by testing applicants sequentially; accepting one precludes later applicants and rejections are irrevocable. It maximizes expected admitted score. (i) With two applicants and the second score uniform on [0,100], what is the first-applicant acceptance threshold? (ii) With three independent uniform scores on [0,100], find the first and, after rejection, second thresholds.
solution: With only the final applicant remaining, expected score is50, so accept the current applicant iff her observed score is at least50. In the three-applicant case the value of rejecting the first is the expected value obtainable from the final two. That value is E[max(X,50)] for X uniform[0,100]: (1/100)[∫₀⁵⁰50 dx+∫₅₀¹⁰⁰x dx]=(2500+3750)/100=62.5. Thus accept the first at score≥62.5; if she is rejected, accept the second at score≥50 and otherwise take the third. At a threshold either decision has equal expected value.
hint: Work backward from the last applicant.
